newsitem.title: GUAM: Families angry at KAL's response in Guam.
newsitem.headline: Families angry at KAL's response in Guam.

text.p: Anguished family members and colleagues of passengers aboard a Korean Air Lines (KAL) jumbo jet which ploughed into a jungle near Guam's airport on Wednesday erupted in anger against the airline.

"It's not apologies and technical information we need now," an elderly man named Kim told KAL vice president Shim Im-taek at a meeting at a hotel in Agana, the capital of this tropical Pacific island.
"Tell us about the fate of our loved ones before discussing blackboxes and such," he said.
The Boeing 747, on a flight from Seoul, South Korea, to Guam with 254 people aboard, crashed as it was trying to land at Guam's international airport early on Wednesday.

The fuselage disintegrated, leaving only the tail section intact. Rescue workers pulled out survivors, and a U.S. military official, Admiral Martin Janczak, said there were 30 survivors and that 69 bodies had been taken out.
But KAL's Shim said he could not confirm the exact number of survivors and could not release any names. The survivors were being treated at two local hospitals.

Shim told the meeting, which was open to the media, that the plane's Digital Flight Data Recorder and the Cockpit Voice Recorder, the two key devices that would shed light on the cause of the crash, were recovered and that the they were already being shipped to Washington D.C. for analysis by the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board.
"I had eight loved ones aboard that flight," another young Korean man shouted at Shim at the meeting. "I want to know that you did everything to rescue them."
"Some people have still a bit of hope here," another middle-aged Korean man said, urging the airline company to publish the names of survivors and those who had perished.
These calls were met with loud applause from the crowd of about 50 family members and colleagues of those aboard Flight 801.
Shim said airline officials were refused entry at the crash site. "It was entirely under the control of the U.S. military. We could not go down to the site. We could only look down upon it."
Shim said the airline company will do its best to confirm the identities of survivors and victims.
